883.title: The field of Siffin
883.hook: Ali's army and Mu'awiyah's meet, Qur'ans are raised on spears, and arbitration is agreed
883.howItsDone: Muslims study Siffin as part of the history of the fitnah; Sunni teaching holds Ali was in the right while counting Mu'awiyah a companion, and Shia Muslims regard Mu'awiyah as a rebel against the rightful Imam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Battle of the Camel, and Ammar, who honored Aisha from the other side. Your line was believers against believers.

Spears go up along a battle line, and on their points are not banners but pages. Pages of the Qur'an. The army holding them is Syrian, led by Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria and a kinsman of Uthman. Facing them is Ali's army. They have fought for days on a plain near the Euphrates, and the histories say Ali's side was pressing hard. Then the pages rise, and a call goes across the field: let the Book of God judge between us.
screen: `SPEARS GO UP.` → `PAGES, NOT BANNERS.` → `LET THE BOOK JUDGE.`

segments.voice: Mu'awiyah had refused to pledge to Ali until Uthman's killers were handed over; Ali held that Mu'awiyah must first accept his caliphate. Neither would move, and the armies met at Siffin. The raised pages, the histories say, were the idea of Amr ibn al-As, on Mu'awiyah's side. A sincere call to the Qur'an, or a way to stop a losing fight? The sources leave room for both readings. Ali, reports say, suspected a stratagem. But soldiers in his own ranks would not fight against the raised pages, and they pressed him to accept. He agreed to arbitration: one man chosen by each side, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari for Ali, Amr ibn al-As for Mu'awiyah, to judge by the Qur'an and the Prophet's way. Bukhari preserves a voice from those days. Sahl ibn Hunayf, who was with Ali, tells his own side: suspect your own opinion. He reminds them of Hudaybiyyah, when the Prophet accepted a truce that looked like a defeat, Umar objected, and the truce turned out to be an opening. A settlement can be right even when it feels like losing. How Muslims judge Siffin differs. In Sunni teaching, Ali was in the right and Mu'awiyah erred in his judgment, while Mu'awiyah is still counted a companion. Shia Muslims see Mu'awiyah as a rebel against the rightful Imam and read the pages as a trick. Either way, the picture stays: pages on the spears, and a battle stopped for words.
screen: `NEITHER WOULD MOVE.` · `AMR'S IDEA, THE HISTORIES SAY.` · `ONE JUDGE FROM EACH SIDE.` · `SUSPECT YOUR OWN OPINION.` · then, large: `PAGES ON THE SPEARS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a standoff where neither side will move first, and notice the voice that says talking now would be losing. Borrow Sahl's words, suspect your own opinion: not dropping it, just holding it more loosely, and picture one small offer to talk. If you pray, you can ask for an open heart in it.
Siffin, the plain near the Euphrates where Ali's army and Mu'awiyah's met, pages of the Qur'an were raised on spears, and arbitration was agreed. Today's word.
Your line: pages on the spears. A text can open talks or close them. Day eight hundred eighty-three, done.

884.title: The Kharijites
884.hook: a group rejects the arbitration, declares others unbelievers, and fights Ali
884.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often use the Kharijites as a warning against takfir, declaring other Muslims unbelievers, and cite the hadith that the charge returns to one of the two.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Siffin, pages raised on spears, and two arbiters chosen. Your line was pages on the spears.

No judgment but God's. In Arabic, la hukma illa lillah. On their face, those are words nobody in Ali's camp would argue with. But a group of his own soldiers starts shouting them at him: you let men judge between you and Mu'awiyah, and judgment belongs to God alone. Some of them, the histories note, were among those who had pushed him to accept the talks in the first place. Now they walk out of his camp and set up their own.
screen: `NO JUDGMENT BUT GOD'S.` → `SHOUTED AT ALI.` → `THEY WALK OUT.`

segments.voice: Kharijites, in Arabic khawarij: those who went out. Ali's answer to their slogan is kept in Sahih Muslim: a word of truth, by which falsehood is intended. The words were true; what they were used for was not. The Kharijites came to hold that anyone who accepted the arbitration had committed a grave sin and was no longer a believer. Ali, they said, had left Islam, and so had anyone who stood with him. Once someone is declared an unbeliever, the histories show how quickly the next step comes. Reports say they killed Muslims on the road who would not condemn Ali. Ali first sent his cousin Ibn Abbas to reason with them, and the reports say some came back. The rest he fought at Nahrawan. The Prophet had warned about this long before. Bukhari records him saying that if a person calls his brother an unbeliever, the word returns to one of the two of them: the charge can land on the one who makes it. Bukhari and Muslim also report the Prophet describing people who would recite the Qur'an without it going past their throats, and Muslim's collection sets that warning beside Ali and the men he faced. A note of fairness: Ibadi Muslims, in Oman and elsewhere, trace part of their history to early dissenters of this time, but they reject the name Kharijite and the extremes it stands for. The lesson the tradition draws is about a single move: declaring.
screen: `KHAWARIJ: THOSE WHO WENT OUT.` · `A WORD OF TRUTH, FOR FALSEHOOD.` · `THE WORD RETURNS TO ONE OF THE TWO.` · `IBADIS REJECT THE NAME.` · then, large: `NOT OUR PLACE TO DECLARE.`

segments.voice: Think of the labels people reach for to put someone outside: fake, sellout, not a real one, not one of us. 885.title: The shield and the judge
885.hook: a well-known report: Ali loses a case against a Christian over a shield, because he has no witness, and the man becomes Muslim
885.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often tell the report of Ali and the judge Shurayh when teaching that rulers stand equal before the law, while noting that hadith scholars have questioned its chain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Kharijites, who went out and declared other Muslims unbelievers. Your line was not our place to declare.

A stall in the market of Kufa, and on it, for sale, a piece of battle gear. A man walking past stops. He knows it. It's his. It went missing, and here it is, in the hands of a Christian trader. The man walking past is Ali, commander of the faithful, ruler of the Muslims. He could have it taken with a word. Instead, the story goes, he says: let's go to the judge. This well-known report is more about the judge than the shield.
screen: `A STALL IN KUFA.` → `THAT'S MINE.` → `LET'S GO TO THE JUDGE.`

segments.voice: The judge is Shurayh, appointed by the caliphs. The caliph walks in as an ordinary party to a case, and in some tellings he gently objects when Shurayh shows him more respect than the other man. Ali says: it's mine. The trader says: it's mine, and it's in my hand. Shurayh asks Ali for witnesses. Ali brings his son Hasan, and in some tellings his servant Qanbar too. The judge says he will not accept a son's testimony for his father. Ali has no further proof, so Shurayh rules for the trader. The caliph lost the case, before his own judge, in his own city. The trader walks out with the gear, then turns back. The ruler of the Muslims, he says, brought me before his own judge, and the judge ruled against him. He says the gear really is Ali's, that it fell from his camel on the road, and he declares himself a Muslim. In the story, Ali gives it to him as a gift. Now the careful part. The report is found in later collections, such as al-Bayhaqi's, and hadith scholars have questioned the strength of its chain. Some tellings make the trader a Jewish man rather than a Christian, and the gear is often a coat of mail rather than a shield. So it's best heard as a report the tradition loves, not a sealed record. What it keeps alive is a command the Qur'an gives: when you judge between people, judge with justice. Shurayh did, even with the caliph standing before him.

886.title: Ali's death
886.hook: Ali is struck in the mosque at Kufa during Ramadan, and asks that his killer be treated fairly (reported)
886.howItsDone: Shia Muslims mourn Ali's wounding and death on nights of Ramadan with prayer and gatherings and visit his shrine at Najaf; Sunni Muslims honor him as the fourth rightly guided caliph and retell his instructions about his killer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the shield and the qadi. Ali lost his claim in court for lack of a witness. Your line was the caliph lost the case.

It is Ramadan, still dark, and people are coming into the mosque at Kufa for the dawn prayer. Ali, the caliph, is among them. So is a man named Ibn Muljam, and he has a sword. He is one of the Kharijites, the ones who declared Ali an unbeliever for agreeing to talk at Siffin. Umar fell at this same hour, in Medina. Now Ibn Muljam strikes Ali on the head. The wound is deep, and Ali is carried home. What he says in the days that follow is the reason this lesson exists.
screen: `DARK, AND RAMADAN.` → `A SWORD AT DAWN PRAYER.` → `CARRIED HOME.`

segments.voice: Reports say that when he was struck, Ali said: by the Lord of the Ka'bah, I have won. Shia and Sunni sources both carry versions of this: a man struck down at prayer, in the month of fasting, counting it as victory. Then come his instructions about the man who did it. The histories, and the letter of counsel to his sons Hasan and Husayn kept in Nahj al-Balagha, give them like this. Keep him well. Feed him, and give him somewhere decent to stay. If I live, I will decide what to do with him; I may forgive him. If I die, then one blow for one blow. Do not kill anyone else on my account. And do not mutilate him, because the Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade mutilation, even of a rabid dog. Set that against the times: a city in turmoil, a ruler struck by a man who called him an unbeliever, and the dying man's worry is that his own side might go too far. No mob, no revenge on a whole tribe. Only what the law allows, with forgiveness left open. Ali died of the wound soon after. Sunni Muslims honor him as the fourth rightly guided caliph. Shia Muslims mourn him as the first Imam, and observe the nights of his wounding and his death in Ramadan with prayer and grief. His shrine at Najaf, in Iraq, is where Shia Muslims hold he is buried, and pilgrims go there. The fitnah was not over, but this is how Ali left it.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has truly wronged you, and notice what you'd like to happen to them. Ask Ali's narrower question: what would be fair, and no more? Let go of the extra blow, the story told to everyone; if you pray, you can leave the rest with God.

887.title: Hasan's peace
887.hook: Hasan makes a treaty with Mu'awiyah to stop the bloodshed, as the Prophet ﷺ foretold (Bukhari)
887.howItsDone: Muslims recall Hasan's treaty with Mu'awiyah through the hadith in Bukhari in which the Prophet calls Hasan a leader through whom God may make peace between two groups of Muslims; Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ali's death. Struck at prayer in Kufa, he asked that his attacker be dealt with fairly. Your line was fair to his killer.

A boy sits beside his grandfather on the pulpit in Medina. The grandfather is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. He looks out at the people, then at the boy, then at the people again, and says: this son of mine is a sayyid, a leader, and perhaps through him God will make peace between two great groups of Muslims. Bukhari keeps the scene. The boy is Hasan, Ali's elder son. Years later, after his father's death, Hasan stands at the head of an army facing another army.
screen: `A BOY ON THE PULPIT.` → `THIS SON OF MINE IS A LEADER.` → `TWO GREAT GROUPS.`

segments.voice: Bukhari keeps the second scene too, in the words of a later narrator, al-Hasan al-Basri. Hasan leads armies he describes as like mountains. Facing him are the forces of Mu'awiyah, the governor of Syria. One of Mu'awiyah's advisers says these armies will not turn back until each has destroyed the other. And Mu'awiyah asks: if these kill those and those kill these, who will be left to look after the people, their families, their affairs? So he sends two men to Hasan, to talk. Hasan listens, and agrees to step aside and make peace. The histories report conditions in the treaty and differ about the details, so the details are best left to them. Bukhari's narrator ties the outcome straight back to the pulpit: through this son, God might make peace between two great groups. Both groups are Muslims. That is what makes the moment heavy. After the Camel and Siffin, believers against believers, a grandson of the Prophet gives up a claim rather than add to the graves. Muslims remember this differently, and fairly. Shia Muslims honor Hasan as the second Imam, and read the treaty as a wise and costly choice made to protect the believers when war would only have destroyed them. Sunni Muslims honor Hasan as a member of the Prophet's household and a companion, and point to this hadith as the Prophet's own praise of what he did. Tradition calls that year the year of unity. The story that began with Ali as caliph ends not on a battlefield, but with a treaty.

888.title: Rule from Damascus
888.hook: Mu'awiyah rules from Damascus, and the caliphate becomes a dynasty
888.howItsDone: Muslims remember the move of the caliphate to Damascus under Mu'awiyah as the start of the Umayyad dynasty; Sunni Muslims honor him as a companion while often criticizing the hereditary turn, and Shia Muslims remember him as Ali's opponent.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hasan's peace. A grandson of the Prophet stepped aside rather than add to the graves. Your line was peace between two groups.

Medina had been the center. The Prophet, peace be upon him, was buried there. Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman had led from there. Ali had moved to Kufa, in Iraq. And now the seat of the Muslim community moves again, north, to an old city: Damascus. The man ruling from there is Mu'awiyah, who had governed Syria under the earlier caliphs. With him, the question that had split the believers since the day after the Prophet's death takes a new shape. Not only who should lead, but how leadership passes on.
screen: `MEDINA, THEN KUFA.` → `NOW DAMASCUS.` → `HOW DOES LEADERSHIP PASS ON?`

segments.voice: Each caliph so far had come to office a different way. Abu Bakr by a pledge in a meeting hall. Umar named by Abu Bakr. Uthman chosen by a council. Ali by a pledge in the mosque, in a crisis. None was a son taking over from a father. The histories report that in his later years Mu'awiyah asked the people to pledge loyalty, in advance, to his son Yazid. Some refused; several sons of the great companions in Medina are reported among them, and so is Husayn. But the pledge was taken, and when Mu'awiyah died, Yazid ruled. The rule of one family, the Umayyads, had begun, passing from father to son, or cousin to cousin, for generations. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says that the caliphate of prophethood would last thirty years, and after it God would give kingship to whom He wills. In Arabic, the word for that kingship is mulk. Some scholars read that hadith against this very moment. Sunni and Shia Muslims see Mu'awiyah differently. Sunni Muslims count him a companion of the Prophet, and Sunni teaching gives him the respect owed to companions, while some Sunni scholars are frank that turning the caliphate into an inheritance was a change for the worse. Shia Muslims see him as the man who fought Ali, the rightful Imam, and who set the stage for the tragedy that came next. Either way, a community that had chosen its leaders now inherited them.

889.title: Husayn refuses
889.hook: Husayn refuses to give his pledge to Yazid and sets out for Kufa with his family
889.howItsDone: Muslims retell Husayn's refusal to pledge to Yazid as the opening of the Karbala story; Shia Muslims honor him as the third Imam, and Sunni and Shia Muslims alike keep the Prophet's words, Husayn is from me and I am from Husayn.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mulk, rule from Damascus, and a pledge to Mu'awiyah's son taken in advance. Your line was a dynasty begins.

A messenger knocks in Medina, at night. The governor wants to see Husayn, now. Mu'awiyah is dead, the histories say, and his son Yazid has written: take the pledge from Husayn, and do not let him put it off. Husayn is the younger son of Ali and Fatima, a grandson of the Prophet, peace be upon him. He goes, and listens, and asks for time: a pledge like this, he says, should be made in public, before the people, not in a room at night. Then he leaves, and before long he leaves Medina altogether.
screen: `A KNOCK AT NIGHT.` → `TAKE THE PLEDGE FROM HUSAYN.` → `NOT IN A ROOM AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: A pledge, a bay'ah, was not a vote. It was a handclasp that bound you to obey. Giving it to Yazid would have meant saying yes to the new shape of power, and Husayn would not give it. The histories follow him to Mecca, where he stays near the Kaaba. Then letters arrive from Kufa, his father's old city, many letters, the reports say, inviting him to come and lead them. He sends his cousin, Muslim ibn Aqil, ahead to see if the welcome is real. Then, against the advice of relatives and friends who are reported to have begged him to stay, he sets out across the desert. Not with an army. With his family: his sisters, his wives, his children, his brothers, and a small circle of companions. Why? Muslims have answered that in different ways. Shia Muslims honor Husayn as the third Imam, and hear in his refusal a stand for the religion itself: a ruler who did not live by it could not be given the believers' hands. Sunni Muslims honor him as a beloved grandson of the Prophet who refused injustice, though some Sunni scholars held that he should have stayed. Tirmidhi keeps a hadith in which the Prophet says: Husayn is from me, and I am from Husayn. A week that began with pages on the spears ends with a man on a road, who would not pledge.
